impervious.definition: Not allowing penetration; unaffected by or unable to be influenced by something
sentences: The fabric was impervious to water, so the hikers stayed dry even through the long afternoon downpour on the mountain trail.
The senator remained impervious to criticism, ignoring every editorial and protest that urged her to reconsider her unpopular stance on the budget.

indiscriminate.definition: Done at random or without careful judgment or selection
sentences: The critic condemned the indiscriminate use of pesticides, which killed beneficial insects along with the harmful pests that farmers were actually trying to eliminate.
Her indiscriminate reading habits meant she devoured cheap romances, technical manuals, and philosophical treatises with equal enthusiasm, never pausing to judge their quality.

infatuate.definition: To inspire with an intense but short-lived passion or foolish love
sentences: The charismatic young actor managed to infatuate half the audience, though most of them forgot his name within a few weeks of the premiere.
Investors were so infatuated with the flashy start-up that they ignored its mounting debts, a passion that faded quickly once the losses became public.
infatuate.mnemonic: In-fatu : fatuus = fou en latin ; on devient fou d'amour.

ingrained.definition: Firmly fixed or deeply rooted and therefore difficult to change
sentences: Her ingrained habit of rising at dawn persisted even after she retired, since decades of early shifts had made it almost impossible to break.
Sociologists argue that prejudice is so deeply ingrained in some communities that it is passed from generation to generation without anyone questioning it.

innocuous.definition: Not harmful or offensive; unlikely to provoke a reaction
sentences: Although the remark seemed innocuous to the speaker, several guests were deeply offended by its hidden implications about their families.
The doctor assured the patient that the small mole was innocuous and posed no threat, so no surgery or further treatment was necessary.

insular.definition: Narrow-minded and uninterested in ideas or people outside one's own group; isolated
sentences: The villagers were so insular that they distrusted every outsider and refused to adopt any custom that had not originated in their own valley.
Critics described the committee as insular, since its members rarely consulted experts from other fields and dismissed any viewpoint that differed from their own.
insular.mnemonic: Insula = île en latin : vivre comme sur une île, coupé du monde.

interplay.definition: The way two or more things affect each other; reciprocal action
sentences: The novel explores the interplay between ambition and guilt, showing how each feeling intensifies the other as the protagonist climbs the corporate ladder.
Biologists study the interplay of genes and environment, since neither factor alone can fully explain why identical twins sometimes develop different personalities.

intricate.definition: Having many small, interconnected parts or details; very complicated
sentences: The watchmaker spent months assembling the intricate mechanism, whose hundreds of tiny gears had to fit together with flawless precision.
Historians struggle to untangle the intricate web of alliances that drew so many nations into the war within only a few weeks.

ironclad.definition: So firmly established that it cannot be broken, challenged, or changed
sentences: The lawyers drafted an ironclad contract with no loopholes, so the company could not escape its obligations even when the market collapsed.
Prosecutors presented an ironclad alibi for the defendant, supported by video footage and several witnesses, and the jury acquitted him within an hour.
ironclad.mnemonic: Iron + clad : revêtu de fer, donc impossible à briser.

jingoistic.definition: Aggressively and excessively patriotic, favoring a belligerent foreign policy
sentences: The tabloid's jingoistic headlines demanded war against the neighboring country and portrayed anyone urging negotiation as a traitor to the nation.
Moderate voters grew uneasy with the candidate's jingoistic speeches, which glorified military power and mocked foreigners while offering no practical plan for the economy.

layman.definition: A person without professional or specialized knowledge in a particular field
sentences: The physicist explained black holes in terms a layman could follow, avoiding equations and technical jargon so the whole audience understood.
Insurance contracts are often written in language so dense that the average layman cannot tell what is actually covered without consulting a lawyer.

levity.definition: Lack of seriousness; humor or frivolity, especially when out of place
sentences: The judge rebuked the lawyer for his levity, insisting that jokes were inappropriate in a courtroom where a man's freedom was at stake.
A moment of levity relieved the tension at the tense negotiations when the mediator cracked a joke, and even the rival delegates laughed.
levity.mnemonic: Levity = lever : léger comme ce qui s'envole ; le contraire de gravity.

loathe.definition: To feel intense dislike or disgust for
sentences: Although she loved the theater, she loathed the long intermissions, which she found tedious and an irritating waste of an otherwise pleasant evening.
Many commuters loathe the morning traffic so intensely that they would gladly accept lower salaries in exchange for jobs within walking distance of home.

lukewarm.definition: Only slightly warm; showing little enthusiasm or interest
sentences: The audience gave the film a lukewarm reception, offering polite applause but none of the excited praise the director had hoped for.
He left the tea sitting so long that it turned lukewarm, neither hot enough to comfort him nor cold enough to refresh him.

lurid.definition: Presented in a shocking, sensational way, often with disturbing detail
sentences: The tabloid printed lurid details of the scandal, hoping that the shocking descriptions would attract more readers than a sober report ever could.
The paperback's lurid cover, with its garish colors and violent imagery, promised a sensational story that the plain, quiet plot never actually delivered.

lush.definition: Growing thickly and abundantly; rich and luxurious
sentences: After weeks of heavy rain, the valley turned lush and green, with thick vegetation covering every hillside and riverbank.
The restaurant's lush decor, with velvet curtains, gilded mirrors, and deep carpets, signaled to diners that the evening would be an expensive indulgence.

mellifluous.definition: Sweet and smooth in sound, pleasant to hear
sentences: The radio host's mellifluous voice soothed listeners so effectively that many admitted they would listen to him read the phone book.
The soprano's mellifluous tones filled the cathedral, and the hushed audience sat spellbound by a sound as smooth and sweet as honey.
mellifluous.mnemonic: Melli- = miel (mel en latin) : une voix qui coule comme du miel.

mores.definition: The customs and accepted behaviors of a particular society or group
sentences: Anthropologists must learn the social mores of a community before studying it, lest they unknowingly violate its traditions and offend the people they hope to understand.
The novel scandalized Victorian readers because it openly challenged the sexual mores of its day, which demanded strict silence on such subjects.

mount.definition: To organize and launch (an effort); to increase gradually in amount or intensity
sentences: The opposition party plans to mount a vigorous campaign against the new tax, beginning with rallies in every major city this spring.
As the deadline approached, the pressure on the engineers continued to mount, and tempers frayed with every day that passed without a working prototype.

multifarious.definition: Having many varied parts, kinds, or forms
sentences: The museum's multifarious collection includes ancient pottery, modern sculpture, rare manuscripts, and even a stuffed dinosaur, so every visitor finds something unexpected.
The mayor faced multifarious problems, from crumbling bridges and unpaid bills to rising crime, and no single policy could address all of them.

nexus.definition: A connection or link between things; a central point where things meet
sentences: Researchers have identified a nexus between poor sleep and weakened immunity, showing that the two problems are closely linked and reinforce one another.
The city, sitting where three major rivers meet, became the nexus of regional trade, drawing merchants from every direction to its crowded markets.

noxious.definition: Harmful or poisonous to health; unpleasant and damaging
sentences: Workers at the chemical plant were required to wear masks because the noxious fumes could damage their lungs after only a few minutes of exposure.
The editorialist argued that the noxious rhetoric of hatred poisoned public debate, harming the whole community even more than the most dangerous pollutants.
noxious.mnemonic: Noxious ressemble à « nocif » : même racine nocere, nuire.

sentences: The small startup had an outsize influence on the industry, shaping standards that much larger rivals felt obliged to follow.
He arrived at the party carrying an outsize bouquet so enormous that he could barely see over it as he squeezed through the door.

overlook.definition: To ignore or excuse (a fault); to fail to notice
sentences: The teacher agreed to overlook the student's late homework this once, because the boy had been ill and had always handed in his work on time before.
Careless investors often overlook hidden fees, which quietly reduce their returns by thousands of dollars over decades because they never read the fine print.

overrun.definition: To invade and spread over in great numbers; to infest
sentences: Within a week, enemy troops had overrun the border towns, forcing thousands of terrified residents to flee toward the capital with whatever they could carry.
After the family abandoned the garden, weeds quickly overran it, choking the flowers and covering the paths until the whole yard looked like a jungle.

overstate.definition: To describe something as greater or more important than it really is
sentences: It would be hard to overstate the importance of the discovery, which transformed medicine and saved millions of lives within a single generation.
The spokesman was accused of trying to overstate the company's profits, inflating the figures to reassure nervous shareholders before the quarterly meeting.

overwhelm.definition: To overpower or defeat completely; to affect so strongly that one cannot cope
sentences: The sheer volume of emails threatened to overwhelm the small staff, who could not possibly answer every message before the end of the week.
Grief can overwhelm even the strongest person, leaving her unable to eat, work, or think clearly for many days after the loss.

parochial.definition: Limited in outlook to narrow local concerns; narrow-minded
sentences: The council's parochial attitude led it to reject the national highway plan, since members cared only about their own village and ignored wider benefits.
Traveling abroad helped cure the student of his parochial view of the world, showing him that his small hometown's customs were not universal.
parochial.mnemonic: Paroisse en français : l'esprit de clocher, qui ne voit pas plus loin.

partial to.definition: Having a particular liking or fondness for
sentences: My grandmother is partial to sweet pastries, and she never lets a visit to the bakery pass without buying at least two of them.
The director was openly partial to older actors, often casting them in leading roles even when younger performers auditioned with more polished technique.
partial to.mnemonic: Partial ≠ partiel ici : on penche d'un côté, on a un faible.

ploy.definition: A clever maneuver or trick used to gain an advantage
sentences: The salesman's offer of a free gift was merely a ploy to get customers into the store, where they would then be pressured to buy.
Critics dismissed the senator's sudden concern for the poor as a political ploy designed to win votes before the election rather than a genuine conviction.

plummet.definition: To fall or drop straight down rapidly
sentences: When news of the scandal broke, the company's share price began to plummet, losing half its value before the markets closed that afternoon.
The injured hawk seemed to plummet from the sky, dropping so swiftly that the watching children gasped before it finally spread its wings near the ground.
plummet.mnemonic: Plomb en français : tomber comme un plomb.

precipitous.definition: Dangerously steep; sudden and rapid, especially of a decline
sentences: The climbers edged along a precipitous cliff, where one wrong step would have sent them tumbling hundreds of feet onto the jagged rocks below.
Economists were alarmed by the precipitous decline in consumer spending, which fell by almost a third within a single month and caught everyone by surprise.

prevailing.definition: Most common or widespread at a particular time; currently in force
sentences: Contrary to the prevailing opinion of the time, which held that the earth was flat, the young astronomer insisted that the world was round.
Sailors rely on the prevailing winds, which blow from the west across the ocean for most of the year, to plan their long voyages.

pristine.definition: In its original, unspoiled condition; perfectly clean and untouched
sentences: The explorers were astonished to find a pristine lake, untouched by tourists or pollution, whose water was so clear they could see the bottom.
Although the vintage car was fifty years old, its pristine paint and spotless leather seats made it look as though it had just left the factory.

proclivity.definition: A natural tendency or inclination, especially toward something undesirable
sentences: His proclivity for gambling worried his friends, who had watched him lose his savings several times and yet return eagerly to the casino.
Psychologists have long debated whether a proclivity for violence is inherited or learned, since both family and environment seem to shape such behavior.

prone.definition: Likely to suffer from or do something; having a tendency toward
sentences: Because the coastal region is prone to flooding, residents build their houses on stilts and keep emergency supplies ready throughout the stormy season.
She was prone to exaggeration, so her friends usually divided any story she told by half before deciding what had actually happened.

proponent.definition: A person who argues in favor of a theory or policy
sentences: As a leading proponent of renewable energy, the senator introduced a bill to fund solar farms and urged colleagues to abandon fossil fuels.
The professor was a staunch proponent of free public education, defending the idea in lectures, newspaper columns, and even in conversations at dinner parties.
proponent.mnemonic: Proponent = qui « propose » et défend une idée ; l'opposé d'opponent.

puzzle.definition: To confuse or perplex by being hard to understand or explain
sentences: The sudden disappearance of the bees continues to puzzle scientists, who have tested dozens of theories without finding a convincing explanation.
His strange refusal to attend the ceremony puzzled his relatives, who knew how long he had worked for the award and could not understand his decision.

remedial.definition: Intended to correct a deficiency or help those who are struggling to learn
sentences: Students who failed the placement test were enrolled in a remedial math course designed to fill gaps in the basic skills they had missed.
The government introduced remedial measures to repair the damage caused by the earlier policy, hoping to correct its worst unintended consequences for rural families.
remedial.mnemonic: Remedial vient de remède : un cours qui soigne les lacunes.

reminisce.definition: To recall and talk about past experiences with pleasure
sentences: The old friends gathered on the porch to reminisce about their college days, laughing at pranks they had not mentioned in decades.
Retired soldiers often reminisce about the camaraderie of the army, remembering the friendships fondly while forgetting many of the hardships they endured.

rendition.definition: A particular performance or interpretation of a song, play, or piece of music
sentences: The pianist's moving rendition of the sonata brought tears to the audience, many of whom said they had never heard the piece played so tenderly.
Critics praised the film as a faithful rendition of the classic novel, preserving its tone and characters while updating the setting for modern viewers.

rescind.definition: To officially cancel or revoke a law, order, or decision
sentences: After widespread protests, the council voted to rescind the controversial parking ordinance, restoring the old rules that residents had preferred.
The university threatened to rescind the scholarship if the student's grades continued to fall, which would make it impossible for her to finish her degree.

revamp.definition: To renovate or improve by making major changes to structure or appearance
sentences: The restaurant plans to revamp its menu and dining room, replacing the tired old decor in a bid to attract a younger crowd.
The editor decided to revamp the struggling magazine completely, redesigning its layout and hiring new writers in hopes of reviving its declining readership.

rote.definition: Done by mechanical repetition without understanding or thought
sentences: Critics of the school system argue that rote memorization of dates and formulas teaches children to repeat facts without ever understanding the underlying ideas.
The clerk answered every question in a rote manner, reciting the same script without listening, so customers left feeling that nobody had actually heard them.

ruffle.definition: To disturb the smoothness or calm of; to upset or irritate
sentences: The unexpected criticism did not ruffle the calm diplomat, who answered each hostile question in the same measured and polite tone as before.
A sudden gust of wind began to ruffle the surface of the pond, breaking the perfect reflection of the trees into countless trembling pieces.

ruthless.definition: Having or showing no pity or compassion; cruel
sentences: The ruthless dictator crushed every protest without mercy, jailing thousands of innocent citizens and showing no compassion even toward the families of his victims.
Known for his ruthless tactics, the executive fired hundreds of loyal employees overnight, caring only about quarterly profits and not at all about their futures.

salable.definition: Fit to be sold; likely to find buyers
sentences: After the flood, only a few pieces of furniture remained salable, and the dealer had to throw away the rest as ruined and worthless.
The publisher rejected the manuscript, not because it lacked merit, but because she doubted that such an obscure poetry collection would be salable to the general public.

salvage.definition: To save or recover something from loss, damage, or destruction
sentences: Divers worked for weeks to salvage valuable cargo from the sunken ship, hoping to recover gold coins before storms covered the wreck with sand.
The coach tried to salvage the team's season by changing tactics, but too many games had been lost for the playoffs to remain realistic.
salvage.mnemonic: Salvage vient de sauver : même racine latine que « salut ».

sentences: The famously shy author seldom gave interviews, so the rare appearance on television drew a much larger audience than the network had expected.
In the desert, rain falls so seldom that when a storm finally arrives, flowers burst into bloom within days and the whole landscape changes color.

serendipity.definition: The happy discovery of something valuable by chance rather than by design
sentences: Pure serendipity led to the discovery of penicillin, when a stray mold happened to contaminate a dish and killed the surrounding bacteria.
It was serendipity that she sat next to the publisher on the train, a chance encounter that eventually led to her first book contract.
serendipity.mnemonic: Les princes de Serendip trouvaient toujours des trésors sans les chercher.

stern.definition: Serious and strict, especially in demanding obedience; severe
sentences: The stern headmaster allowed no talking in the corridors and punished even minor offenses, so students feared his stare more than any detention.
Her father gave her a stern warning never to drive without a license, and his grave expression made clear that he was not joking.

stopgap.definition: A temporary solution used until a permanent one can be found
sentences: The city built a wooden footbridge as a stopgap while engineers designed a permanent structure to replace the bridge that the flood had destroyed.
Critics said the subsidy was merely a stopgap that would postpone the crisis without resolving the deeper problems that had caused the industry's decline.
stopgap.mnemonic: Stop + gap : on bouche un trou en attendant mieux.

suit.definition: To be appropriate or becoming for; to befit
sentences: The somber tone of the music did not suit the cheerful wedding, and several guests exchanged puzzled glances as the band began to play.
Her calm and patient temperament suits her well for a career in nursing, where steady empathy is needed more than quick wit.

sweeping.definition: Wide-ranging and extensive in effect; radical, often too broad or general
sentences: The new president announced sweeping reforms that would transform the tax code, the healthcare system, and the education budget within only two years.
The historian cautioned against sweeping generalizations about the era, noting that the lives of peasants, merchants, and nobles differed far too much for one description.

tawdry.definition: Showy but cheap and of poor quality; sordid
sentences: The carnival's tawdry decorations, made of cheap plastic and flaking gold paint, looked glamorous at night but shabby in the harsh light of morning.
Critics dismissed the reality show as a tawdry spectacle that exploited its contestants' private misery to entertain viewers with gossip and cheap drama.
After the long hike, the tepid water from the old canteen was far from refreshing, but the thirsty travelers drank it gratefully.
The proposal received only tepid support from the board, whose members offered polite nods but declined to commit any money to the project.

trappings.definition: The outward signs or symbols associated with a role, status, or office
sentences: Although he enjoyed the trappings of success, such as the luxury car and the corner office, he privately felt his work had little meaning.
The prime minister's residence, with its uniformed guards and gilded rooms, displayed all the trappings of power that the voters had once criticized.

typify.definition: To be a characteristic example of; to embody
sentences: The small stone cottage with its thatched roof and flower garden seems to typify the rural English countryside that tourists love to photograph.
Critics say the senator's refusal to compromise typifies the stubborn partisanship that has paralyzed the legislature and prevented even modest agreements for years.

understated.definition: Presented in a subtle, restrained way rather than being showy
sentences: Her understated elegance, a plain black dress and a single pearl necklace, drew more admiration than the flashy outfits of the other guests.
The novelist's understated prose never raises its voice, yet the quiet restraint makes the tragic events of the story feel all the more powerful.

uptick.definition: A small or modest increase, especially in a statistic or business figure
sentences: Analysts noted a slight uptick in consumer confidence last month, though it was too small to suggest that the long recession had truly ended.
The hospital reported an uptick in flu cases after the holidays, a modest rise that officials expected to subside by the end of winter.

verisimilitude.definition: The appearance of being true or real; believability in fiction
sentences: The author gave her fantasy novel a surprising verisimilitude by including realistic details about food, weather, and money, so readers believed in its invented kingdom.
Film historians admire the director's commitment to verisimilitude, noting that he insisted on authentic costumes and dialect so that the period drama would appear genuine.
verisimilitude.mnemonic: Veri- (vrai) + similis (semblable) : semblable au vrai, donc vraisemblance.

vicarious.definition: Experienced in the imagination through the actions or feelings of another person
sentences: Never having traveled herself, she took vicarious pleasure in her sister's adventures, reading every letter as though she were walking through those distant cities.
Many parents live vicariously through their children, hoping the young athletes will achieve the glory that they themselves were never able to win.
vicarious.mnemonic: Vicarius = remplaçant : vivre à la place d'un autre (le vicaire).

vivid.definition: Producing strong, clear images in the mind; bright and intense in color
sentences: The veteran gave such a vivid account of the battle that listeners could almost hear the cannons and smell the smoke drifting across the field.
The artist favored vivid reds and yellows, and her canvases glowed so brightly that they seemed to light up even the darkest corners of the gallery.
